name: The five remembrances
summary: Each day, recollect slowly: I am subject to ageing; to illness; to death; I will be parted from all that is dear; I am the owner of my actions, and will inherit them. Let each one sink in before the next.

steps.text: Each day, recollect slowly: I am subject to ageing; to illness; to death; I will be parted from all that is dear; I am the owner of my actions, and will inherit them.
Let each one sink in before the next.

contraindications: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

name: Mindfulness of death (maranasati)
summary: At nightfall and daybreak, reflect that death could come tonight or today from many causes, and ask whether any unskilful quality is still unabandoned. Let the urgency feed effort, not fear.

steps.text: At nightfall and daybreak, reflect that death could come tonight or today from many causes, and ask whether any unskilful quality is still unabandoned.

name: Recollecting the round
summary: Contemplate how long the round of birth and death has been, and how many losses it holds, until disenchantment with becoming arises. Then turn to the breath and rest.

name: Powa: an introduction to transference at death
summary: Read a traditional introduction before seeking instruction from a qualified teacher: refuge, visualising Amitabha above the crown, and training the mind's direction at death. It is taught with empowerment, not from a page.

name: Preparing for the bardo
summary: Notice the small gaps of daily life (falling asleep, the pause between thoughts) as rehearsals for the great transition, and rest there as awareness.

name: Self-enquiry: who dies?
summary: When the thought of death comes, ask to whom it comes. Trace the 'I' back to its source instead of following the thought. Ramana's own awakening began by lying down and enacting his death.

name: Practising dying (melete thanatou)
summary: Socrates calls philosophy the practice of dying: loosening the soul's grip on the body's pleasures and fears, day by day. Read the Phaedo slowly as an exercise, not an argument.

name: Analytic meditation on the stages of the path
summary: Pick one Lamrim topic, such as the preciousness of this human life or the certainty of death. Think it through step by step, using reasons and examples, until a felt conviction comes. Then rest single-pointedly on that conviction for a while. Alternate thinking and resting.

name: Self-enquiry
summary: Whenever a thought arises, ask to whom it arises; the answer is 'to me'; then ask 'who am I?' and hold attention on the sense of I.

steps.text: Whenever a thought arises, ask to whom it arises; the answer is 'to me'; then ask 'who am I?' and hold attention on the sense of I.

name: Contemplating not-self
summary: Take each aggregate in turn and ask: is it constant, is it easeful, is it fitting to regard it as me, mine, my self?

steps.text: Take each aggregate in turn and ask: is it constant, is it easeful, is it fitting to regard it as me, mine, my self?

name: Shiva Process self-inquiry
summary: Bring to mind a situation that is troubling you. Describe what you feel in plain words, then ask "what is the deeper feeling under this?" and keep going, layer by layer, until something shifts and the contraction releases. Often done in pairs or with a guide.

name: "What am I? Don't know"
summary: Ask "What am I?" deeply on the in-breath. On the out-breath, hold "Don't know..." as long as the breath lasts. Return to this don't-know mind in every activity, and keep clear about the next correct action. This is Seung Sahn's Kwan Um teaching.

name: Owner of my actions
summary: The fifth remembrance: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions. Recollect it before acting and after.

steps.text: The fifth remembrance: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions.

name: Mindfulness of breathing
summary: Sit comfortably, know the in-breath and out-breath, then let the breath calm the whole body before turning to feelings and mind.

steps.text: Sit comfortably, know the in-breath and out-breath, then let the breath calm the whole body before turning to feelings and mind.

contraindications: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

name: Goodwill (metta)
summary: Wish yourself well, then widen the wish to others, near and far, seen and unseen, without exception.

steps.text: Wish yourself well, then widen the wish to others, near and far, seen and unseen, without exception.

name: Resting in the gap between breaths (Vijñāna Bhairava dhāraṇā)
summary: Sit comfortably and breathe naturally. Notice the instant where the in-breath turns into the out-breath, and the instant where the out-breath turns back. Do not hold the breath; simply let attention fall into each turning point and rest there for its brief duration. Over time, notice the open awareness that is present in the pause.

name: Recognition (pratyabhijñā) contemplation
summary: Read one sūtra of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam slowly. Then look at present experience — a sound, a thought, a feeling — and ask whether anything appears outside awareness. Let the understanding "this too is a form of the one consciousness" settle as a felt recognition rather than an idea. Return to the text, then to experience, alternating.

name: Drawing the Śrī Chakra as meditation
summary: Following a teacher's step-by-step construction, draw the Śrī Yantra slowly from the centre point (bindu) outward: the nine interlocking triangles, the lotus rings and the square gateways. Treat each stage as a contemplation of the goddess unfolding into the world, not as geometry homework.

name: Basic Śaiva Siddhānta meditation
summary: Sit upright, regulate the breath to a slow even count, then draw awareness inward from the senses to the spine and to the inner light, holding a single point of focus. Hinduism Today's monastery teaches it as part of daily worship and study.

name: Mantra repetition (japa)
summary: Choose a mantra received from your tradition, sit with a mala, and repeat it at an even pace, aloud, whispered or mentally. Let attention rest on the sound and its meaning; when the mind wanders, return to the next repetition.

steps.text: Choose a mantra received from your tradition, sit with a mala, and repeat it at an even pace, aloud, whispered or mentally.

name: Ānāpānasati (breath meditation, "Method 2")
traditionLabel: Dhammayut forest line (Ajahn Mun → Maha Boowa / Ajaan Lee)
summary: Sit upright and notice the breath at whatever point it is clearest. Let it settle into a comfortable rhythm, then let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath energy as a home base for steady, alert attention.

name: "Buddho" recollection
summary: Silently repeat "bud-" on the in-breath and "-dho" on the out-breath to anchor the mind; when the mind is calm, drop the word and stay with the knowing itself. Used widely in the Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah lines.

name: Walking meditation (jongrom)
traditionLabel: Ajahn Chah line (Wat Nong Pah Pong)
summary: Choose a straight path of 15–30 paces. Walk at a natural or slow pace, attention on the feet or the whole body; at each end, stop, turn, and re-collect before walking back.

name: Mahasi noting
summary: Watch the rise and fall of the abdomen and give each event a soft mental label ("rising", "falling", "thinking", "hearing"), then return to the primary object; move to slow walking with labels for lifting, moving and placing.

name: Natural awareness (right attitude)
summary: Instead of forcing focus on one object, relax and know whatever is being experienced, checking the attitude of the observing mind (craving, aversion, impatience) throughout daily activities.

name: Satipaṭṭhāna (four establishings of mindfulness)
summary: Contemplate body, feeling, mind and mental qualities as they arise and pass, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, without greed or distress about the world (MN 10).

name: RAIN
summary: Recognise what is happening; Allow it to be there; Investigate with kindness how it feels in the body; Nurture with self-compassion; then rest in the awareness that remains.

name: Open awareness (shamatha without a support)
summary: After a few minutes with a support, let it go. Leave the eyes open and the gaze soft. Let sights, sounds and thoughts come and go, and do not follow them or push them away. When you get caught up, simply notice it and relax again. The point is to rest as the knowing that is already present.

name: Looking at the mind (Mahamudra)
summary: Once the mind is calm, turn and look for the one who is looking. Ask where a thought comes from, where it stays, and where it goes. Do not reason about it; just look and rest in whatever is seen or not found. This practice is traditionally done under a qualified teacher's guidance.

name: Resting in rigpa (Dzogchen), orientation only
summary: In Dzogchen, the student is introduced to the nature of mind (rigpa) by a teacher. Between sessions, practitioners recall that recognition, leave it uncontrived for short moments, many times, and release any effort to improve it. This entry describes the practice and is not a substitute for the introduction itself.

name: Shikantaza (just sitting)
summary: Sit as in zazen, but drop counting and any object. Simply sit, aware of the whole posture and the whole field of experience, without chasing or suppressing anything. When you find yourself lost in thought, come back to the posture. Dogen treats the sitting itself as realisation, not as a means to it.

name: Koan practice with Mu
summary: Take up "Does a dog have buddha nature? Mu" (Zhaozhou). Breathe Mu on each exhalation and put your whole doubt into it. Do not interpret it. Present your understanding to a teacher in private interview (dokusan). Koan work depends on that meeting with a teacher.

name: Silent illumination (mozhao)
summary: Relax the body and be aware of the whole body sitting. Widen that awareness to include the environment, without any centre or edge. Silence means not adding commentary; illumination means remaining clearly aware. Rest there, and return whenever you get caught.

name: Bhairavi Sadhana (Isha)
summary: A lay devotional observance offered by the Isha Foundation around Linga Bhairavi: for a set period the practitioner keeps simple disciplines (as given by Isha), offers daily devotion to the goddess, and completes it with an offering at a Linga Bhairavi abode. The exact rules come from the organisation each year.

name: Śravaṇa–manana–nididhyāsana
summary: Systematic listening to the Upaniṣads with a teacher (śravaṇa), resolving doubts by reflection (manana), and dwelling on the understood meaning until it is assimilated (nididhyāsana).

summary: Repeat a mantra or name of God given by the teacher, often with a mālā of 108 beads, letting the mind rest in its meaning and the feeling of devotion.

name: Hare Krishna mahāmantra (japa and kīrtan)
summary: Chant "Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare / Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare" softly on beads (japa) or sing it together (kīrtan), as practised since Chaitanya.

name: Nembutsu / nianfo
summary: Recite "Namu Amida Butsu" (Japanese) or "Namo Amituofo" (Chinese), aloud or silently, with a mala if you like. In Chinese Pure Land, recitation is a practice of concentration and aspiration for rebirth. In Shin Buddhism, it is an expression of gratitude for Amida's vow, not a means of earning anything.

name: Christian meditation with a mantra (Maranatha)
summary: Sit still and upright with your eyes lightly closed. Silently repeat one prayer-word, "Ma-ra-na-tha", in four equal syllables, listening to it rather than thinking about its meaning. When thoughts or images arrive, return to the word, without force. Sit for 20–30 minutes, morning and evening.

name: Centering Prayer
summary: Choose a sacred word as a sign of consent to God's presence. Sit comfortably and bring it in gently. When you notice you are engaged with a thought, return ever so gently to the word. End by resting in silence for a couple of minutes. Twice daily, 20 minutes.

name: Lectio Divina
summary: Read a short scripture passage slowly, then again; notice the word that catches you; respond to it in prayer; rest in silence. Read, ponder, pray, rest.

name: The Jesus Prayer (prayer of the heart)
summary: Repeat "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" slowly and attentively, often with a prayer rope, keeping the mind in the words and letting it descend into the heart. Begin with a fixed time each day; humility and stillness come before technique.

summary: Sitting quietly, repeat the phrase of divine unity (La ilaha illa'llah) aloud or silently, letting the breath and a gentle movement of the head carry it, until the remembrance continues on its own in the heart.

summary: Join a short divine name or phrase to the in- and out-breath; keep attention on the heart; finish with silence and a prayer.

name: Khatm-i Khwajagan (Naqshbandi group dhikr)
summary: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

summary: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

name: Calming and contemplation (zhiguan)
summary: First calm the mind (zhi) by settling the breath and posture. Then contemplate (guan) any present thought as simultaneously empty, provisionally existing, and the middle, which are the threefold truth. Zhiyi's Mohe zhiguan sets out four kinds of samadhi practice (constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking half-sitting, and neither).

name: Rudi's double breath
summary: Breathe in, bringing attention down from the throat into the heart, and then down to the navel and the base of the body. Breathing out, let the energy rise up the spine. Keep the movement gentle and continuous, and return to the heart when attention scatters.

name: Khecarī mudrā (historical description only)
summary: Described in haṭha texts as turning the tongue back and up into the cavity above the soft palate, sometimes after gradually lengthening the tongue. We list it for context: the full form involves cutting the frenum and is not something to try from a video.

name: Dream yoga, first steps
summary: During the day, keep reminding yourself "this is a dream" so that the habit carries into sleep. Before sleep, set a strong intention to recognise dreams. Visualise a luminous syllable at the throat as you fall asleep. Each morning, review whether you recognised a dream, and renew the intention.

name: Feeding your demons (a modern adaptation of Chöd)
summary: Find a struggle, such as fear or a craving, and feel where it lives in the body. Picture it as a figure in front of you and ask what it wants and what it really needs. Then imagine dissolving your body into nectar that gives it exactly that, until it is satisfied. Rest in the open space that remains.

name: The view from above (spiritual exercise)
summary: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters. One of the ancient "spiritual exercises" Pierre Hadot described.

summary: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

name: Active imagination / imaginal attention
summary: Stay with an image (from a dream, a text or a place) as a living presence; let it speak and move; respond to it honestly rather than interpreting it away. In Corbin's terms it is a perception of the mundus imaginalis.

name: Neelakantha Meditation (mantra-based)
summary: This is an initiated mantra practice: the mantra is received from an authorised teacher. In outline, one sits twice a day, repeats the given mantra inwardly and lets it become subtle, treating the body as a stable platform rather than an obstacle. name: Nyāsa — placing mantra on the body
summary: Touch or attend to specific points of the body (heart, head, crown, arms) while silently repeating the syllables assigned to them, so the body is treated as a seat of the deity before worship or meditation. Traditionally learnt with the specific mantra from a teacher.

name: Contemplating the Twelve Kālīs (Krama)
summary: Take one Kālī of the Krama sequence at a time (e.g. Sṛṣṭikālī, the Kālī of creation). Study what phase of cognition she stands for — an object arising, being held, being withdrawn into the knower — and watch that phase in your own experience during the day.

name: Mettā (loving-kindness)
summary: Wish well to yourself, then a benefactor, a friend, a neutral person, a difficult person and finally all beings, using simple phrases or a felt sense of goodwill, letting it spread in every direction.

name: Body sweeping (Goenka vipassanā)
summary: After a few days of ānāpāna to sharpen attention, move attention systematically through the body from head to feet, observing every sensation with equanimity, as taught in ten-day residential courses.

name: Yoga nidrā
summary: Lying down, rotate awareness through the body, then breath, opposite sensations and visualisations while staying awake, ending with a personal resolve (saṅkalpa).

name: Five points of yoga (Sivananda)
summary: Proper exercise (āsana), proper breathing (prāṇāyāma), proper relaxation, proper diet and positive thinking with meditation, as summarised by Swami Vishnudevananda.

name: Breath-centred, individually adapted āsana (viniyoga)
summary: Link every movement to a slow inhale or exhale and adapt sequence, length and intensity to the person's body, age and aims, as taught by Krishnamacharya and T. K. V. Desikachar.

name: Calm abiding with a support
summary: Sit upright and relaxed. Rest your attention lightly on a simple support, such as the breath at the nostrils, a pebble, or a sound. When you notice the mind has wandered, return to the support without scolding yourself. Aim for many short, clear sessions rather than a few long, dull ones. Over time, loosen your grip until attention rests on its own.

name: Tonglen (sending and taking)
summary: Flash briefly on open, spacious mind. Then breathe in a feeling of heaviness and heat, and breathe out a feeling of coolness and light. Start with a real person who is suffering, perhaps yourself, and breathe in their pain while breathing out relief. Widen this to everyone who feels the same. Keep it simple and close to how you actually feel.

name: Mind training (lojong) slogans
summary: Choose one of the 59 slogans of Atisha's Seven Points, such as "Drive all blames into one". Carry it through the day. When irritation or self-cherishing comes up, recall the slogan and look again at the situation. Review the day each evening.

name: Nine breathings of purification
summary: Visualise the three channels: a central blue channel with a white one on the right and a red one on the left. Breathe in through the right nostril and out through the left three times, releasing anger. Then breathe in through the left and out through the right three times, releasing attachment. Finally, breathe in through both and push the breath up the central channel three times, releasing ignor

steps.text: Visualise the three channels: a central blue channel with a white one on the right and a red one on the left.
Breathe in through the right nostril and out through the left three times, releasing anger.
Then breathe in through the left and out through the right three times, releasing attachment.
Finally, breathe in through both and push the breath up the central channel three times, releasing ignorance.
Rest afterwards.

contraindications: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

name: Zazen posture and breath
summary: Sit on a cushion with your knees on the floor, or on a chair, with the spine upright. Rest the hands in the cosmic mudra, left on right with the thumbs lightly touching, and keep the eyes half-open and lowered. Breathe naturally through the nose. Beginners can count breaths from one to ten and start again whenever they lose count.

name: Huatou (critical phrase)
summary: Take up a short question, such as "What is wu?" or "Before my parents were born, what was my original face?" Keep asking it with a sense of genuine not-knowing until a "great doubt" gathers. Return to the question whenever you lose it. This is Sheng Yen's method, best done in retreat with guidance.

name: Mindful breathing with gathas
summary: Breathe in and silently say "In"; breathe out and say "Out". As you settle, shorten it to "Deep / Slow", "Calm / Ease" or "Smile / Release". Use a bell or a phone chime as a reminder to stop, breathe three times and come back to the body.

name: Walking meditation
summary: Walk slowly and coordinate your steps with your breath, for example two steps on the in-breath and three on the out-breath. Feel each foot touching the earth as if kissing it. You are not trying to arrive anywhere; every step is the arrival.

name: Ajikan (A-syllable meditation)
summary: Shingon practitioners visualise the Sanskrit syllable A on a moon disc above a lotus. The A signifies the unborn source of all things. They join it with the breath and expand the moon until it fills the universe, then contract it into the heart. Formal ajikan is taught after initiation; this entry is an orientation only.

name: Video lectio (short contemplative reading)
summary: Watch a short image or text slowly, then sit with a single phrase that stays with you before meditating.

name: Welcoming Practice
summary: When a strong reaction arises, feel it as a sensation in the body; say "welcome" to it instead of resisting; then let go of the desire for security, approval or control, and so release it into presence.

name: Neoplatonic contemplation ("strip away everything")
summary: Following Plotinus, turn attention from objects to the activity of knowing, then let even that subtle self-image fall away, resting in the simple presence it comes from. Usually practised after a period of calming meditation.

name: Letter-combination meditation (ecstatic Kabbalah)
summary: Abulafia's path: combine and permute the Hebrew letters of divine names, with breath and pronunciation, to loosen ordinary thinking. Historically taught only under a teacher. Listed here for context, not as instruction.
